![Illustration: Edmon De Haro for [The Wall Street Journal](https://apple.news/ARhMogxwxQTGTRDCFgWsXvA).](cover.jpg){fig-align="center"}

[A WSJ essay](https://apple.news/ARhMogxwxQTGTRDCFgWsXvA) by theoretical neuroscientist [Vivienne Ming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vivienne_Ming), reporting on her experiment that pitted humans alone, AI models alone (ChatGPT and Gemini), and human–AI hybrids against Polymarket's prediction market.

> As a neuroscientist, I conducted research into artificial versus human intelligence. The results surprised me—and suggest we've been worrying over the wrong things.

Only 5–10% of hybrid teams actually beat the market. They treated the AI as a **sparring partner**, demanding evidence, asking for counterarguments, pushing back when it sounded confident. Most hybrids instead rubber-stamped the model's answer or used it to ratify their own priors (classic confirmation bias plus sycophancy), and performed no better than the AI alone. The qualities that separated the winners were perspective-taking and intellectual humility, both fundamentally emotional skills. Ming names the deeper risk the **Information-Exploration Paradox**: as the cost of information approaches zero, human exploration collapses.

## My Notes

Ming's most underrated claim is the one buried near the end: nearly all AI benchmarks measure what AI agents can do alone. The entire field optimizes against scoreboards that reward solo performance, which inevitably trains labs to build products that make the human optional rather than sharper. A hybrid-intelligence benchmark, scored on what the pair produces together relative to either component alone, would change what counts as an improvement. [Anthropic's Economic Index](/posts/20260423-anthropic-economic-index/) recently surfaced one version of that measurement: the Claude.ai task time horizon is 19 hours with human steering, against the same model's 2 hours when running autonomously on METR's benchmark. That 5× gap comes from the human bringing task decomposition, judgment about what to attempt, and verification mid-flight. It is exactly the hybrid-intelligence delta Ming is arguing the field should be measuring directly.

The sparring-partner pattern is also where decades of cognitive-science literature have the most to add. [Philip Tetlock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_E._Tetlock)'s **superforecasters**, the top ~2% of volunteers identified by accuracy across a multi-year IARPA forecasting tournament, exhibit active open-mindedness and treat their own forecasts as tentative hypotheses, revising them when new evidence arrives. That disposition is exactly what the 5–10% of hybrid cyborgs were doing with their AI. If Ming is right about which qualities separate the winners, the field already has research on how to cultivate them in individuals, and tools like calibration training could transfer to the human half of the hybrid directly. She doesn't make that connection explicit.

The Information-Exploration Paradox is probably more useful as a population-level claim than an individual one. At the individual level, the students who arrive with good metacognitive habits may use AI to skip the easy struggle and spend their friction budget on harder ideas, while the students who don't may skip the struggle entirely. The paradox may not apply uniformly. It may widen existing gaps along lines that already correlate with educational outcomes. The prescription then becomes less "design AI that preserves friction" and more "design AI that scaffolds the metacognitive moves that separate the cyborgs from the rubber-stampers" — the [scaffold-not-substitute](/posts/20260130-ai-coding-scaffold-not-substitute/) distinction Anthropic found in its coding study.

The hardest unresolved tension in the piece is commercial. Most AI revenue today comes from removing friction, which means a product that preserves it loses to the one that doesn't in head-to-head adoption. The AI Ming wants to see built is probably not going to come out of consumer chatbots at all. It will come from tutoring, [coaching](/posts/20260412-coachgpt-marathon/), and domain-expert tools where the user is explicitly paying for the struggle to be preserved. Duolingo and ChatGPT both use AI, but only one is structurally set up to build the capacities she is arguing for.
